title: Streaks, honestly
hookLine: streaks can motivate, but a broken one can make people quit

cards: A little flame next to a number, glowing on a phone screen. Every day the number goes up by one, and every day there's a small pull to keep it going. Then a flight, a fever, a funeral, and the number drops back to zero.
What happens next? Some people shrug and start again. Some close the app and never open it.
Researchers have started to look at that second response, and what they've found cuts both ways.

teach.h: A CHAIN CAN HELP YOU SHOW UP.
teach.b: First, the good side. Counting days in a row can help. A visible chain gives a small reason to show up today, and it makes progress easy to see.
Nothing wrong with that. Second, the break. The consumer researchers Jackie Silverman and Alixandra Barasch studied what happens when a streak ends.

teach.h: A BROKEN STREAK CAN MAKE PEOPLE QUIT.
teach.b: In their studies, a broken streak often led people to pull back from the activity afterward, as if the lost number had become the point.
Earlier, the dieting researchers Janet Polivy and Peter Herman described something similar: after one slip, some dieters stopped holding back altogether. They nicknamed it the what-the-hell effect.

Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, a classic text of yoga, say that practice, abhyasa, becomes firmly grounded when it is kept up for a long time, without break, and with devotion. A streak counts only one of those three.
It can't see a long practice that has a gap in it, and it can't see devotion at all. Fourth, honest use.

A streak is a tool, not a verdict. If it helps you show up, keep it. If a broken one makes you want to quit, that's the moment to remember that the curve forgives, and that the count was never the practice.
The breath you take tomorrow doesn't know what number it is.

how: Some people use a day count to keep a practice going and treat a break as a pause rather than a failure; others leave counting out entirely and simply return each day.

o: a count of days in a row, useful but not the practice
a measure of how deeply you practiced each day
a reward you earn once a habit is fully formed

s: a broken streak never changes what people do next
in Silverman and Barasch's studies, a broken streak often led people to pull back.
the Yoga Sutras name more than 'without break' for grounded practice
they also name a long time and devotion.
a visible chain can be a small reason to show up.

games.q: your streak just broke during a family emergency. which next step fits today's lesson?
o: delete the app so it can't happen again.
sit today and let the count start wherever it starts.
wait until you can manage a perfect run.
games.why: the risk the research points to is pulling back after the break. coming back keeps the practice, whatever the counter says.

practice: For this sit, don't count breaths, minutes or days. If a number shows up, how long it's been, how many days in a row, label it 'counting' and come back to the breath you're on. Only this one breath is here to be practiced.

wordCard.voice: Streaks. A count of days in a row: useful as a nudge, risky when it breaks, and never the practice itself. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, from Patanjali's Yoga Sutras: steady, repeated practice.

carryVoice: Your line: not the streak. The part that matters most is the part no number can see. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Silverman & Barasch, "On or off track: How (broken) streaks affect consumer decisions"
